newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans protest against liberal abortion law.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans protest against liberal abortion law.

text.p: Anti-abortion activists protested across South Africa on Sunday against a draft law that would change the country's abortion law from one of the world's toughest to one of the most liberal.
More than 3,000 people overflowed the Durban City Hall to oppose passage of the Termination of Pregnancy Bill currently before parliament in Cape Town.
"This is the most permissive piece of abortion legislation in the world and we are deeply angry about that," Albie van Eeden, president of Doctors for Life, told Reuters.
"Our government is on the brink of crossing the line to legalised violence in the most intimate of relationships, that beteen a mother and her child," he said.
In Cape Town, anti-abortion protesters lined the entrance to the popular Waterfront tourist district with posters saying "Abortion kills babies".
A teenaged girl carried a poster with photographs of babies ripped apart during late-term abortions.
The latest survey amongst 3,300 people showed on Sunday that only one in four South Africans supports abortion on demand.

"It shouldn't even be in the minds of people, because it's killing," nursing sister Bertha Lechaba told Reuters at a mass demonstration by at least 2,000 Christians on the lawns outside President Nelson Mandela's Union Buildings offices in Pretoria.
Organiser Ed Cain appealed to Mandela to scrap the abortion bill or allow a public vote.

Parliament will this month debate Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma's proposal for state-financed abortion on demand during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy and for a further eight weeks if physical or emotional risk, rape, sexual abuse, and severe social or economic consequences are involved.
The bill proposes that minors should be allowed abortions without their parents' knowledge or consent and specifically denies husbands and fathers a say.
Aligned to the government's pro-choice approach are women's rights groups which have campaigned for over 20 years for the abortion laws to be relaxed.
"It is something that is the lesser of two evils. For many women it's a last resort," said Michelle O'Sullivan of the Reproductive Rights' Alliance.
Only about 1,000 women a year qualify for legal abortions under current law allowing termination under circumstances such as incest, rape or danger to the mother's life.

South Africa's Medical Research Council says close to 50,000 women report to hospitals every year after botched backstreet abortions from which over 400 die. Unofficial estimates however are that 120,000 women procure illegal abortions every year.

"The reality in South Africa is about improving the quality of women's lives so they have access to employment... in a way that isn't going to affect their health and impact on the rest of their family," O'Sullivan said.
"If women have wide access to contraception and pre-natal care, it will bring down the rate of abortion -- because then unwanted pregnancies can become planned pregnancies."
A minority right-wing group, the Boerestaat Party, lambasted the ruling African National Congress over the proposed abortion law recently, accusing it of plotting to exterminate Afrikaners.
"It is a calculated plan to cut our numbers and as such is nothing short of ethnic cleansing," the party claimed.
Public hearings on the divisive issue start on October 14.
